title: Direct calculation for maximum product cutting
summary: Use integer division and remainder to write n = 3 × a + b and adjust the split by remainder case, handling small cases n = 2 and n = 3 separately so at least two parts are formed.
context: Given an integer n ≥ 2, split n into at least two positive integers summing to n to maximize their product.

Because the optimal greedy strategy extracts as many 3s as possible, the code avoids cutting in a loop and instead computes quotient a = n // 3 and remainder b = n % 3 in one step to get the count a of 3s and remainder b.
description: The diagram decomposes a bar of length n into "a copies of 3" and a "Remainder b" segment above the identity n = 3 × a + b (with a = n // 3 and b = n % 3 in {0, 1, 2}). Drawing "Remainder b" on the left is purely symbolic—neither fixing concrete values of n or b nor implying left-to-right cutting—while ellipses between blue 3-blocks stand for additional copies of 3.

The table below supplies all five cases from the chapter text and code (not drawn separately in the figure). Boundary inputs n = 2 and n = 3 must be cut into at least two parts rather than left uncut as n.

When n ≥ 4 and b = 1, we have a ≥ 1, so at least one 3 can be recombined with remainder 1 into 2 + 2—keeping sum 4 while raising their local product from 3 to 4—leaving a - 1 copies of 3 and product 3^(a - 1) × 2 × 2 (3 raised to the exponent (a minus 1), times 2 times 2).

frames.title: Compute the maximum product directly by cases on quotient a and remainder b
frames.explanation: In the figure, "Remainder b" represents the quotient-remainder decomposition: b = 0 leaves no remainder piece, b = 2 keeps 2 as a factor, and b = 1 recombines with one 3 as in the table—0 is never used as a factor.
